notes.title: Key facts by topic
notes.html:
Equations & inequalities

  • Undo, in reverse — To solve an equation, undo what was done to x, in reverse order. Whatever you do to one side, do to the other.
  • Variables on both sides — Move the x terms to one side and the numbers to the other. Then divide by the coefficient.
  • Distribute first — Multiply the number outside the parentheses by EVERY term inside. Then solve like normal.

Linear functions

  • Slope — Slope tells how steep a line is: rise over run. Up-right is positive; down-right is negative.
  • Slope-intercept form — In y = mx + b, m is the slope and b is where the line crosses the y-axis.
  • Make a line from a point — Use the slope and a point to find b: plug x and y into y = mx + b, then solve for b.

Systems

  • What is a solution? — A solution of a system is the point that makes BOTH equations true. On a graph it is where the lines cross.
  • Substitution — Solve one equation for a letter, then plug that into the other equation. Best when a letter is already alone.
  • Elimination — Add or subtract the equations so a letter cancels. Multiply an equation first if needed.

Exponents

  • Multiply, same base — When multiplying powers with the same base, ADD the exponents.
  • Power of a power — For (xᵃ)ᵇ, MULTIPLY the exponents. Also raise every factor inside the parentheses.
  • Divide, same base — When dividing, SUBTRACT the exponents (top minus bottom).

Factoring

  • Factor out the GCF — Find the biggest number and letters shared by every term and pull them out. Always do this first.
  • Trinomials x² + bx + c — Find two numbers that multiply to c and add to b. They go in the two parentheses.
  • Difference of squares — a² − b² always factors into (a − b)(a + b). There must be a minus sign between two squares.

Radicals

  • Square roots — √a asks: what number times itself gives a? Perfect squares: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81, 100.
  • Simplify a radical — Pull out the biggest perfect square factor. √72 = √36 · √2 = 6√2.
  • Multiply and divide — √a · √b = √(ab). You can also split a root of a fraction into top and bottom.

Quadratics & functions

  • Function notation — f(x) is the output for input x. To find f(3), replace every x with 3 and calculate.
  • Quadratic shape — The graph of y = ax² + bx + c is a parabola. If a > 0 it opens up; if a < 0, down.
  • Vertex — The vertex is the turning point. Its x-coordinate is −b/(2a). Plug in to get y.

Points, lines, angles

  • Point, line, plane — A point is a location. A line goes on forever in two directions. A plane is a flat surface that goes on forever.
  • Segment and ray — A segment has two endpoints. A ray has one endpoint and goes on forever. Name a ray with its endpoint first.
  • Naming and measuring angles — An angle has a vertex and two sides. Acute < 90°, right = 90°, obtuse between 90° and 180°, straight = 180°.

Logic & proof

  • If–then statements — 'If p, then q.' p is the hypothesis and q is the conclusion. A statement is true only if it can never fail.
  • Converse, inverse, contrapositive — Converse: swap p and q. Inverse: negate both. Contrapositive: swap AND negate. Only the contrapositive always matches the original.
  • Counterexamples — One example that makes the hypothesis true and the conclusion false proves a statement false.

Parallel lines & polygons

  • Parallel lines and a transversal — A transversal crosses two lines and makes 8 angles. With parallel lines, corresponding, alternate interior and alternate exterior angles are EQUAL.
  • Same-side interior — Same-side interior angles between parallel lines add to 180°. Z shape means equal, C shape means supplementary.
  • Prove lines parallel — The converses work: if corresponding or alternate interior angles are equal, the lines are parallel.

Congruent triangles

  • Congruent triangles — Congruent triangles are the same shape AND size. Matching parts are called corresponding parts.
  • Four ways to prove it — SSS, SAS, ASA and AAS prove congruence. For right triangles, HL works. AAA and SSA do NOT.
  • CPCTC — After you prove triangles congruent, ALL their matching parts are congruent. This is how you prove segments or angles equal.

Quadrilaterals

  • Parallelogram properties — Opposite sides are parallel and equal, opposite angles are equal, consecutive angles add to 180°, diagonals bisect each other.
  • Prove a parallelogram — Show ONE of: both pairs of opposite sides equal, one pair both parallel and equal, or diagonals bisect each other.
  • Rectangle — A parallelogram with four right angles. Its diagonals are equal.

Similarity

  • Ratio and proportion — A ratio compares two numbers. A proportion says two ratios are equal. Cross-multiply to solve.
  • Similar figures — Same shape, different size. Corresponding angles are equal and corresponding sides are in the same ratio (the scale factor).
  • Prove triangles similar — AA is enough. Also SAS∼ (two sides in proportion, included angle equal) and SSS∼ (all three sides in proportion).

Right triangles & trig

  • Pythagorean theorem — In a right triangle, the legs squared add to the hypotenuse squared. The hypotenuse is opposite the right angle.
  • Pythagorean triples — Whole-number triples show up often: 3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17, 7-24-25. Multiples work too.
  • 45-45-90 — The legs are equal and the hypotenuse is leg × √2.

Circles

  • Circle vocabulary — Radius: center to the circle. Chord: two points on the circle. Diameter: chord through the center. Tangent: touches once. Secant: cuts twice.
  • Central angles and arcs — A central angle has the same measure as its arc. A full circle is 360°.
  • Inscribed angles — An inscribed angle is HALF its intercepted arc. An angle in a semicircle is 90°.

Constructions & loci

  • The tools — Classic constructions use only a compass and straightedge. The compass copies equal lengths.
  • Copy a segment or angle — Set the compass to the length and mark it off. For an angle, copy the arc and the chord that cuts it.
  • Bisectors — Arcs from both ends with equal radii cross at two points. The line through them is the perpendicular bisector.

Area

  • Rectangle and parallelogram — Rectangle: length × width. Parallelogram: base × height, where height is perpendicular to the base.
  • Triangle — A triangle is half of a parallelogram. Use any side as the base with its matching height.
  • Trapezoid — Average the two bases and multiply by the height.

Solids

  • Prisms and cylinders — Volume = base area × height. Lateral area is the sides only; total surface area adds the bases.
  • Pyramids and cones — Volume is one third of a prism or cylinder with the same base and height.
  • Spheres — Surface area 4πr². Volume (4/3)πr³.

Coordinate geometry

  • Distance formula — The distance between two points comes from the Pythagorean theorem.
  • Midpoint — Average the x's and average the y's.
  • Slope — Rise over run. Parallel lines have equal slopes. Perpendicular lines have slopes that multiply to −1.

Transformations

  • Isometries — Translations, reflections and rotations keep size and shape. A dilation keeps shape but changes size.
  • Translation — Slide every point the same way. Add the shift to each coordinate.
  • Reflection — Flip over a line. Over the x-axis: (x, −y). Over the y-axis: (−x, y). Over y = x: (y, x).

written: Explain why the angles of a triangle add to 180°.
Draw a line through one vertex parallel to the opposite side. Alternate interior angles are equal, so the three angles sit along a straight line (180°).
Why is AAA not enough to prove triangles congruent?
Three equal angles make the same SHAPE but can be any SIZE, so the triangles are only similar.
What does an indirect proof assume first?
The opposite of the statement you want to prove. Then you show it leads to a contradiction.
How do you decide between SAS and ASA?
Look at what is between: SAS has an angle between two sides; ASA has a side between two angles.
Cut an equilateral triangle in half. The short leg is half the side, the hypotenuse is the full side, and the long leg is short leg × √3.
bench: Measure your height and your shadow, then a tree's shadow at the same time. Use similar triangles to find the tree's height.
Draw a triangle, tear off the three corners and place them together. They make a straight line.
Measure the circumference and diameter of three round objects. Divide. Each answer should be near 3.14.
checklist: Bring pencils and a calculator if allowed.
Show your work on free-response items.
Check answers by plugging back in.

questions.q: What does AAS tell you about two triangles?
o: They are congruent if two angles and a side NOT between them match
They are congruent if three angles match
sol: AAS: two angles and a side NOT between them are congruent.
Matching three ANGLES (AAA) does not prove congruence.
questions.w: Matching three ANGLES (AAA) does not prove congruence.

questions.q: What does ASA tell you about two triangles?
o: They are congruent if two angles and the side BETWEEN them match
They are congruent if three angles match
sol: ASA: two angles and the side BETWEEN them are congruent.
Matching three ANGLES (AAA) does not prove congruence.
questions.w: Matching three ANGLES (AAA) does not prove congruence.

questions.q: What does SAS tell you about two triangles?
o: They are congruent if two sides and the angle BETWEEN them match

questions.q: What does HL tell you about two triangles?
o: They are congruent if hypotenuse and a leg (right triangles) match
They are congruent if three angles match
sol: HL: hypotenuse and a leg (right triangles) are congruent.
Matching three ANGLES (AAA) does not prove congruence.
questions.w: Matching three ANGLES (AAA) does not prove congruence.

questions.q: What does SSS tell you about two triangles?
o: They are congruent if three pairs of sides match
They are congruent if three angles match
They are congruent if two sides match
sol: SSS: three pairs of sides are congruent.
Matching three ANGLES (AAA) does not prove congruence.
questions.w: Matching three ANGLES (AAA) does not prove congruence.

questions.q: Which pair of facts is NOT enough to prove two triangles congruent?
sol: AAA only gives the same SHAPE, not the same size.
SSS, SAS, ASA and AAS all force the same size.
questions.w: SSS, SAS, ASA and AAS all force the same size.

sys: A solution of a system is the point that makes BOTH equations true. On a graph it is where the lines cross.
Solve one equation for a letter, then plug that into the other equation. Best when a letter is already alone.
Add or subtract the equations so a letter cancels. Multiply an equation first if needed.
Parallel lines (same slope, different b) give NO solution. Same line gives infinitely many.
Plug your (x, y) into BOTH original equations. If both work, you are done.
exp: When multiplying powers with the same base, ADD the exponents.
For (xᵃ)ᵇ, MULTIPLY the exponents. Also raise every factor inside the parentheses.
When dividing, SUBTRACT the exponents (top minus bottom).
Anything (not 0) to the 0 is 1. A negative exponent means flip to the other side of the fraction.
Write a number as a × 10ⁿ with 1 ≤ a < 10. Moving the decimal left makes n bigger.
fac: Find the biggest number and letters shared by every term and pull them out. Always do this first.
Find two numbers that multiply to c and add to b. They go in the two parentheses.
a² − b² always factors into (a − b)(a + b). There must be a minus sign between two squares.
For ax² + bx + c, try the product a·c and split the middle term, then group.
If a product equals 0, one factor must be 0. Set each factor equal to 0 and solve.
rad: √a asks: what number times itself gives a? Perfect squares: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81, 100.
Pull out the biggest perfect square factor. √72 = √36 · √2 = 6√2.
√a · √b = √(ab). You can also split a root of a fraction into top and bottom.
Only LIKE radicals combine, just like like terms. Simplify first.
If a root is left in the denominator, multiply top and bottom by that root.
qdr: f(x) is the output for input x. To find f(3), replace every x with 3 and calculate.
The graph of y = ax² + bx + c is a parabola. If a > 0 it opens up; if a < 0, down.
The vertex is the turning point. Its x-coordinate is −b/(2a). Plug in to get y.
Move everything to one side, factor, set each factor to 0.
When factoring fails, use the formula. The discriminant b² − 4ac tells how many real solutions.
Repeated percent change uses A = P(1 + r)ⁿ. Decay uses (1 − r).
Arithmetic adds the same number each time; geometric multiplies by the same number.
|x| is the distance from 0. |x − 3| = 5 means x is 5 away from 3, so two answers.
bas: A point is a location. A line goes on forever in two directions. A plane is a flat surface that goes on forever.
A segment has two endpoints. A ray has one endpoint and goes on forever. Name a ray with its endpoint first.
An angle has a vertex and two sides. Acute < 90°, right = 90°, obtuse between 90° and 180°, straight = 180°.
Complementary add to 90°. Supplementary add to 180°. A linear pair is two adjacent angles that make a straight line.
When two lines cross, the angles directly across from each other are equal.
A midpoint splits a segment into two equal parts. A bisector splits a segment or angle in half.
Reflexive: a = a. Symmetric: if a = b then b = a. Transitive: if a = b and b = c then a = c. Substitution lets you swap equals.
log: 'If p, then q.' p is the hypothesis and q is the conclusion. A statement is true only if it can never fail.
Converse: swap p and q. Inverse: negate both. Contrapositive: swap AND negate. Only the contrapositive always matches the original.
One example that makes the hypothesis true and the conclusion false proves a statement false.
Inductive finds a pattern from examples and may be wrong. Deductive uses facts to reach a sure conclusion, like in a proof.
Each statement needs a reason: given, definition, postulate or theorem. Start with the givens; finish with what you prove.
Assume the opposite of what you want. Show it leads to a contradiction. Then the original must be true.
par: A transversal crosses two lines and makes 8 angles. With parallel lines, corresponding, alternate interior and alternate exterior angles are EQUAL.
Same-side interior angles between parallel lines add to 180°. Z shape means equal, C shape means supplementary.
The converses work: if corresponding or alternate interior angles are equal, the lines are parallel.
The three angles of a triangle always add to 180°. An exterior angle equals the sum of the two remote interior angles.
Interior angle sum = (n − 2) × 180°. Exterior angles of any convex polygon add to 360°.
A regular polygon has equal sides and equal angles. Each exterior angle = 360° ÷ n.
tri: Congruent triangles are the same shape AND size. Matching parts are called corresponding parts.
SSS, SAS, ASA and AAS prove congruence. For right triangles, HL works. AAA and SSA do NOT.
After you prove triangles congruent, ALL their matching parts are congruent. This is how you prove segments or angles equal.
Equal sides have equal angles opposite them, and the other way around. The bisector of the vertex angle is also a median and an altitude.
A median goes to a midpoint, an altitude is perpendicular, an angle bisector splits an angle. The medians meet at the centroid.
Any two sides add to MORE than the third. The longest side is opposite the largest angle.
Perpendicular bisectors meet at the circumcenter; angle bisectors at the incenter; altitudes at the orthocenter.
quad: Opposite sides are parallel and equal, opposite angles are equal, consecutive angles add to 180°, diagonals bisect each other.
Show ONE of: both pairs of opposite sides equal, one pair both parallel and equal, or diagonals bisect each other.
A parallelogram with four right angles. Its diagonals are equal.
A parallelogram with four equal sides. Its diagonals are perpendicular and bisect the angles.
A square is both a rectangle and a rhombus, so it has every one of those properties.
One pair of parallel sides (bases). The midsegment is parallel to the bases and equals their average.
Two pairs of equal adjacent sides. One diagonal is the perpendicular bisector of the other.
sim: A ratio compares two numbers. A proportion says two ratios are equal. Cross-multiply to solve.
Same shape, different size. Corresponding angles are equal and corresponding sides are in the same ratio (the scale factor).
AA is enough. Also SAS∼ (two sides in proportion, included angle equal) and SSS∼ (all three sides in proportion).
A line parallel to one side of a triangle cuts the other two sides in proportion.
An angle bisector in a triangle divides the opposite side in the same ratio as the two sides next to it.
If the scale factor is k, perimeters scale by k and areas scale by k². Volumes scale by k³.
rt: In a right triangle, the legs squared add to the hypotenuse squared. The hypotenuse is opposite the right angle.
Whole-number triples show up often: 3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17, 7-24-25. Multiples work too.
The legs are equal and the hypotenuse is leg × √2.
Short leg x, long leg x√3, hypotenuse 2x.
In a right triangle, the altitude to the hypotenuse is the geometric mean of the two pieces. Each leg is the geometric mean of the hypotenuse and its adjacent piece.
SOH-CAH-TOA: sin = opp/hyp, cos = adj/hyp, tan = opp/adj. Label sides from the angle you are using.
Both angles are measured from the horizontal. They make alternate interior angles, so they are equal.
cir: Radius: center to the circle. Chord: two points on the circle. Diameter: chord through the center. Tangent: touches once. Secant: cuts twice.
A central angle has the same measure as its arc. A full circle is 360°.
An inscribed angle is HALF its intercepted arc. An angle in a semicircle is 90°.
A tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of touching. Two tangents from one outside point are equal.
Inside the circle: half the SUM of the arcs. Outside: half the DIFFERENCE of the arcs.
Two chords: part × part = part × part. Tangent: (tangent)² = whole secant × outside part.
con: Classic constructions use only a compass and straightedge. The compass copies equal lengths.
Set the compass to the length and mark it off. For an angle, copy the arc and the chord that cuts it.
Arcs from both ends with equal radii cross at two points. The line through them is the perpendicular bisector.
Use equal arcs to make a perpendicular from a point. Copying a corresponding angle makes a parallel line.
A locus is ALL points that satisfy a rule. Equidistant from two points: a perpendicular bisector. At distance r from a point: a circle.
To satisfy two rules, draw each locus and mark where they cross. Count the intersections.
area: Rectangle: length × width. Parallelogram: base × height, where height is perpendicular to the base.
A triangle is half of a parallelogram. Use any side as the base with its matching height.
Average the two bases and multiply by the height.
Area = ½ × apothem × perimeter. The apothem goes from the center to the middle of a side.
Circumference = 2πr. Area = πr². Keep π in your answer for an exact value.
A sector is a fraction of the circle: angle/360. Multiply that fraction by the area or circumference.
If lengths scale by k, area scales by k².
sol: Volume = base area × height. Lateral area is the sides only; total surface area adds the bases.
Volume is one third of a prism or cylinder with the same base and height.
Cylinder lateral area = 2πrh. Total area adds two circles: 2πr² + 2πrh.
With scale factor k, surface areas scale by k² and volumes by k³.
Pyramids and cones use the slant height for lateral area. Find it with the Pythagorean theorem.
crd: The distance between two points comes from the Pythagorean theorem.
Average the x's and average the y's.
Rise over run. Parallel lines have equal slopes. Perpendicular lines have slopes that multiply to −1.
Center (h, k), radius r. Note the signs: the center's coordinates are subtracted.
Place a figure on axes with smart coordinates (a vertex at the origin). Use distance, slope or midpoint to prove properties.
Check side lengths and slopes. Equal and parallel opposite sides → parallelogram. Add right angles → rectangle.
trn: Translations, reflections and rotations keep size and shape. A dilation keeps shape but changes size.
Slide every point the same way. Add the shift to each coordinate.
Flip over a line. Over the x-axis: (x, −y). Over the y-axis: (−x, y). Over y = x: (y, x).
Turn about a point. About the origin: 90° → (−y, x), 180° → (−x, −y), 270° → (y, −x).
A figure has line symmetry if a flip maps it onto itself. It has rotational symmetry if a turn less than 360° maps it onto itself.
A dilation multiplies coordinates by the scale factor k. Doing transformations one after another is a composition.

glossary: A line that crosses two or more lines.
Angles in the same position at each crossing.
Angles between the lines on opposite sides of the transversal.
Corresponding parts of congruent triangles are congruent.
The point halfway along a segment.
Cuts something into two equal parts.
The side opposite the right angle.
One of the two sides forming the right angle.
A segment from a vertex perpendicular to the opposite side.
A segment from a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side.
A segment with both endpoints on a circle.
A line touching a circle at one point.
An angle whose vertex is on the circle.
From the center of a regular polygon to the middle of a side.
The set of all points that fit a rule.
A transformation that scales a figure.
The statement with hypothesis and conclusion swapped.
Swap and negate the hypothesis and conclusion.
A statement that has been proven.
The number multiplied by a variable.
Rise over run; how steep a line is.
A corner point; also the turning point of a parabola.
b² − 4ac; tells how many real solutions a quadratic has.
A closed figure made of segments.
stuck: Write what you KNOW and what you must FIND.
Draw and label a picture. Mark equal parts.
Pick a theorem or formula that links them. Then check if the answer is sensible.

proofs.title: Vertical angles are equal
proofs.given: Lines ℓ and m intersect; ∠1 and ∠3 are vertical angles; ∠2 is between them.
proofs.idea: Both angles are supplements of the SAME angle (∠2). Things that are supplementary to the same angle must be equal.
proofs.deep: This is the "same-supplement" pattern: if two angles are each supplementary to one angle, they are congruent. Notice the proof never uses the picture, only the postulates, so it works for every pair of crossing lines.
proofs.trap: Do not write "vertical angles are equal" as a reason inside this proof — that is what you are proving.

proofs.title: The angles of a triangle add to 180°
proofs.given: △ABC.
steps: Through C draw line ℓ parallel to AB
Parallel postulate: exactly one parallel through a point
Name the angles on ℓ: ∠4 beside ∠A-side and ∠5 beside ∠B-side
Alternate interior angles of parallel lines are congruent
Angles along a straight line (ℓ) add to 180°
proofs.idea: Add one helper line. A line through C parallel to the base turns the triangle angles into three angles lying along a straight line.
proofs.deep: The parallel postulate is essential. In spherical geometry no such parallel exists and triangle angles add to MORE than 180°, which is why this proof is a real piece of Euclidean geometry.
proofs.trap: Alternate interior angles are only equal because the lines are parallel — you built the parallel line, so you earned that fact.

proofs.title: Base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal
proofs.given: △ABC with AB = AC; D is the midpoint of BC.
steps: CPCTC (corresponding parts of congruent triangles are congruent)
proofs.idea: To show two angles equal, put them in two triangles you can prove congruent, then use CPCTC.
proofs.deep: A different route uses the angle bisector from A and SAS. Both rely on adding an auxiliary segment — the key skill for harder proofs is deciding what to draw.
proofs.trap: CPCTC is the LAST step. You may only use it after the triangles are proven congruent.

proofs.title: A point on the perpendicular bisector is equidistant from the endpoints
proofs.given: Line ℓ is the perpendicular bisector of AB at M; P is on ℓ.
proofs.idea: The two small triangles on each side of ℓ share side PM. Matching the bisected segment and the right angles gives SAS.
proofs.deep: The converse is also true and is how compass constructions work: points equidistant from A and B lie on the perpendicular bisector. Together they say "the perpendicular bisector is exactly the set of equidistant points" — a locus statement.
proofs.trap: Make sure the angle sits BETWEEN the two sides you use. Here ∠PMA is between PM and MA — that is why it is SAS.

proofs.title: Opposite sides of a parallelogram are congruent
proofs.given: Parallelogram ABCD (AB ∥ DC and AD ∥ BC).
proofs.idea: A diagonal cuts the parallelogram into two triangles. Parallel sides give two pairs of equal angles, and the diagonal is shared.
proofs.deep: The same diagonal cut proves opposite ANGLES are equal. Many parallelogram facts come from this single congruence.
proofs.trap: Name the congruent triangles with vertices in matching order: △ABC ≅ △CDA, not △ABC ≅ △ACD.

proofs.title: Diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other
proofs.given: Parallelogram ABCD; diagonals meet at E.
steps: Opposite sides of a parallelogram are congruent
proofs.idea: Two triangles formed by the crossing diagonals are congruent because the parallel sides AB and DC give equal angles.
proofs.deep: Reverse it: if diagonals of a quadrilateral bisect each other, it is a parallelogram. That converse is a standard way to PROVE a shape is a parallelogram in coordinate geometry.
proofs.trap: The sides you use for ASA must be between the angles: AB is between ∠BAE and ∠ABE.

proofs.title: Midsegment of a triangle
proofs.given: △ABC; D and E are midpoints of AB and AC.
steps: Equal corresponding angles force parallel lines
Corresponding sides of similar triangles are proportional
proofs.idea: Midpoints give a 1 : 2 ratio on two sides plus a shared angle — exactly SAS similarity with scale factor ½.
proofs.deep: This is a special case of the side-splitter theorem. With coordinates you can verify it by the midpoint and slope formulas, which is a good second proof to compare.
proofs.trap: SAS ∼ needs the ratios equal and the INCLUDED angle equal; here ∠A is between the two sides.

proofs.title: The Pythagorean theorem (similar triangles proof)
proofs.given: Right △ABC with right angle at C; altitude CD to hypotenuse AB. Let AB = c, BC = a, CA = b.
steps: AA similarity (each pair shares an acute angle and has a right angle)
proofs.idea: The altitude to the hypotenuse makes two small triangles similar to the big one. Each leg is the geometric mean of the hypotenuse and the piece next to it.
proofs.deep: This proof shows WHY: it also gives the three "geometric mean" relations used in rt problems: leg² = hypotenuse × adjacent piece, altitude² = product of the two pieces.
proofs.trap: Write similarity in matching order (△ABC ∼ △CBD) or your ratios will be crossed.

proofs.title: Inscribed angle theorem (center on one side)
proofs.given: Circle O; inscribed ∠ABC with BC a diameter (O on BC).
steps: All radii of a circle are equal
A central angle equals its intercepted arc
proofs.idea: Hide an isosceles triangle inside the circle using two radii. Its exterior angle is the central angle and doubles the base angle.
proofs.deep: The other two cases (center inside, center outside) are handled by drawing the diameter through B and adding or subtracting two copies of this case. That "reduce to a special case" idea shows up all over mathematics.
proofs.trap: The inscribed angle must have its VERTEX on the circle. A vertex at the center gives a central angle instead.

proofs.title: A tangent is perpendicular to the radius (indirect proof)
proofs.given: Line t is tangent to circle O at T.
steps: Assume OT is NOT perpendicular to t
Draw OP ⊥ t with P on t, P ≠ T
Through a point not on a line there is exactly one perpendicular
Choose Q on t so that P is the midpoint of TQ
Points T and Q are equidistant from O (△OPT ≅ △OPQ by SAS)
Q is on the circle, so t meets the circle twice
Q is on circle O since OQ = OT = radius
This contradicts that a tangent meets the circle in exactly one point
proofs.idea: Suppose the radius is slanted. Then you can find a second point of the line on the circle — but a tangent touches only once. Contradiction.
proofs.deep: Indirect proof (proof by contradiction): assume the opposite, derive something impossible, conclude the original claim. It is the right tool when the statement is a "not" or "only one" claim.
proofs.trap: In an indirect proof the first line is the NEGATION of what you want, not what you want.

proofs.title: √2 is irrational (Honors indirect proof)
proofs.given: √2 is a real number.
proofs.prove: √2 is not a fraction of whole numbers
steps: Square both sides; multiply by b²
a² is even, so a is even
If a² is even then a is even
b² is even, so b is even
a and b are both even, so the fraction was not in lowest terms
So √2 cannot be written as a/b
proofs.idea: Assume it is a fraction in lowest terms. Squaring shows both top and bottom are even — impossible in lowest terms.
proofs.deep: This is one of the oldest proofs (ancient Greece). It matters in geometry: the diagonal of a unit square is √2, so lengths exist that no ratio of whole numbers can measure — a big shock to early mathematicians.
proofs.trap: "Lowest terms" is what makes the contradiction work. Without it, both being even is not a problem.

proofs.title: Why AAS works (from ASA)
proofs.given: △ABC and △DEF with ∠A ≅ ∠D, ∠B ≅ ∠E, BC = EF (side not between the angles).
steps: m∠C = 180° − m∠A − m∠B and m∠F = 180° − m∠D − m∠E
proofs.idea: If two angles match, the third must match too. That turns a side NOT between two angles into a side that IS between two angles.
proofs.deep: This is why AAS needs no separate postulate. It also explains why AAA is not enough: three equal angles say nothing about size.
proofs.trap: Any matching side works for AAS, because the third angle is forced to match as well.

proofs.title: Exterior angle is bigger than either remote angle
proofs.given: △ABC with exterior angle ∠ACD at C (D on extension of BC).
steps: An angle of a triangle has positive measure
Substitution; a sum of positives exceeds one part
proofs.idea: The exterior angle equals the sum of the two remote angles, so it is bigger than each one by the measure of the other.
proofs.deep: This inequality powers the triangle inequality theorem and the "larger angle opposite larger side" theorem, so it sits at the base of Chapter 4 style arguments.
proofs.trap: Remote interior angles are the two NOT touching the exterior angle.

proofs.title: Alternate interior angles equal means the lines are parallel
proofs.given: Lines ℓ and m are cut by transversal t. Alternate interior angles ∠1 and ∠2 are congruent. ∠3 is the vertical angle of ∠2.
steps: If corresponding angles are congruent, the lines are parallel
proofs.idea: Turn the angle pair you have into the pair a postulate talks about (corresponding angles).
proofs.deep: This is the converse of the alternate interior angles theorem. The Corresponding Angles Postulate is accepted without proof; every other parallel-line test is built from it plus vertical angles.
proofs.trap: Do not use “alternate interior angles are congruent” as a reason when you are trying to prove lines parallel. That is the theorem for parallel lines, not the test.

proofs.title: If two angles of a triangle are equal, the sides opposite them are equal
proofs.given: △ABC with ∠B ≅ ∠C. Draw the bisector of ∠A meeting BC at D.
proofs.idea: Build two triangles that share a side, prove them congruent, then read off the equal sides.
proofs.deep: This is the converse of the isosceles triangle theorem. Notice the bisector gives the “extra” angle pair needed for AAS; a perpendicular from A would also work.
proofs.trap: You need the shared side AD as the non-included side for AAS. The angle at D is not given, so SAS would be wrong.

proofs.title: The diagonals of a rhombus are perpendicular
proofs.given: Rhombus ABCD with diagonals meeting at E.
steps: Diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other
They lie on the straight line AC
Congruent angles that form a linear pair are right angles
proofs.idea: Equal sides give congruent triangles; congruent angles on a straight line must be 90°.
proofs.deep: A rhombus is a parallelogram, which is why the diagonals bisect each other. The same congruence also shows each diagonal bisects the angles at its ends.
proofs.trap: A rectangle has bisecting diagonals too, but they are not perpendicular. Perpendicularity comes from the equal sides.

proofs.title: The diagonals of a rectangle are congruent
proofs.given: Rectangle ABCD with diagonals AC and BD.
steps: Opposite sides of a parallelogram are congruent
proofs.idea: Find two triangles that contain the diagonals as corresponding sides.
proofs.deep: The triangles are △ABC and △DCB: they share BC, have equal legs AB and DC, and equal included right angles. The converse is also true: a parallelogram with congruent diagonals is a rectangle.
proofs.trap: Check that the angle is between the two sides you use. Here the right angle at B is between AB and BC, so SAS applies.

proofs.title: If both pairs of opposite sides are equal, the quadrilateral is a parallelogram
proofs.given: Quadrilateral ABCD with AB = CD and AD = BC.
steps: If alternate interior angles are congruent, the lines are parallel
If alternate interior angles are congruent, the lines are parallel
proofs.idea: A diagonal splits the figure into congruent triangles, and congruent triangles give you parallel-line angle pairs.
proofs.deep: This is the converse of the theorem you proved earlier (opposite sides of a parallelogram are congruent). Together they show the two properties are equivalent.
proofs.trap: The order of letters matters in △ABC ≅ △CDA: A matches C and B matches D.

proofs.title: A line parallel to one side of a triangle divides the other two sides proportionally
proofs.given: △ABC with D on AB and E on AC, and DE ∥ BC.
steps: Corresponding sides of similar triangles are proportional
AB = AD + DB and AC = AE + EC
proofs.idea: Parallel lines give equal angles, equal angles give similar triangles, and similar triangles give proportions.
proofs.deep: The result is the Side-Splitter Theorem. Its converse (equal ratios imply parallel) is also true and is proved with similar triangles and the corresponding angles test.
proofs.trap: The proportion AD/AB = AE/AC compares part to whole. To get part to part you need the substitution step.

proofs.title: Altitude to the hypotenuse: h² = xy
proofs.given: Right △ABC with right angle at C. CD ⊥ AB at D, AD = x, DB = y, CD = h.
steps: The acute angles of a right triangle are complementary
The acute angles of a right triangle are complementary
Complements of the same angle are congruent
Corresponding sides of similar triangles are proportional
proofs.idea: The altitude cuts the big right triangle into two smaller ones that are similar to each other.
proofs.deep: The same figure gives the other two geometric means: AC² = x·AB and BC² = y·AB. Adding them gives the Pythagorean theorem a second proof.
proofs.trap: Match vertices in the right order when writing △ADC ∼ △CDB, or the proportion will flip.

proofs.title: Converse of the Pythagorean theorem (Honors)
proofs.given: △ABC with side lengths a, b, c and a² + b² = c².
steps: Build right △DEF with legs a and b and hypotenuse x
Take the positive square root (lengths are positive)
proofs.idea: You cannot assume the triangle is right. Build a right triangle you know, show it has the same sides, and use SSS.
proofs.deep: This is why the 3-4-5 rope trick works for builders. It also gives the test for acute and obtuse triangles: if a² + b² > c² the triangle is acute; if less, obtuse.
proofs.trap: Do not start by writing “a² + b² = c² because it is a right triangle”. That assumes what you must prove.

proofs.title: A radius perpendicular to a chord bisects the chord
proofs.given: Circle with center O. Radius OM ⊥ chord AB at P.
steps: All radii of a circle are congruent
proofs.idea: Draw the radii to the chord’s endpoints to make two right triangles with equal hypotenuses.
proofs.deep: The converse also holds: the line from the center to the midpoint of a chord is perpendicular to it. Together they explain why the perpendicular bisector of any chord passes through the center.
proofs.trap: HL needs a right angle, a hypotenuse and one leg. OA and OB are the hypotenuses, OP is the shared leg.

proofs.title: Tangent segments from an outside point are congruent
proofs.given: P is outside circle O. PA and PB are tangent to the circle at A and B.
steps: A tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of tangency
All radii of a circle are congruent
proofs.idea: Two radii to the tangent points make two right triangles that share the hypotenuse OP.
proofs.deep: This is why a circle inscribed in a triangle has equal tangent lengths from each vertex, the basis of many Honors perimeter problems.
proofs.trap: The right angles come from the theorem about tangents and radii, so that theorem must be cited as a reason first.

proofs.title: Opposite angles of an inscribed quadrilateral are supplementary
proofs.given: Quadrilateral ABCD is inscribed in a circle.
steps: An inscribed angle is half its intercepted arc
An inscribed angle is half its intercepted arc
The arcs of a full circle add to 360°
m∠A + m∠C = ½·(arc BCD + arc BAD)
proofs.idea: Each angle uses the arc on the far side from it; those two arcs together fill the circle.
proofs.deep: The converse gives a test: a quadrilateral whose opposite angles are supplementary can be inscribed in a circle (cyclic).
proofs.trap: Use the arc that is opposite the angle (the one it sees), not the arc between the angle’s sides on the near side.

proofs.title: An exterior angle equals the sum of the two remote interior angles
proofs.given: △ABC with D on the extension of BC beyond C.
proofs.idea: Both sums equal 180°, so set them equal and cancel the shared angle.
proofs.deep: This theorem is the engine behind the Exterior Angle Inequality and many angle-chasing problems on contests.
proofs.trap: The “remote” angles are the two interior angles that are NOT adjacent to the exterior angle.

proofs.title: Coordinate proof: diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other
proofs.given: Parallelogram with vertices O(0, 0), A(a, 0), B(a + b, c), C(b, c).
proofs.prove: The diagonals OB and AC bisect each other
steps: Place the parallelogram with O at the origin and OA on the x-axis
The two midpoints are the same point
Each diagonal passes through the midpoint of the other
proofs.idea: Choose coordinates that make the algebra easy, then compute with formulas instead of drawing triangles.
proofs.deep: Coordinate proofs use variables for general shapes: a, b, c stand for any parallelogram, so one calculation covers all of them. Placing a vertex at (0, 0) and a side on the x-axis is the standard first move.
proofs.trap: Using specific numbers like (3, 4) would only prove the statement for one parallelogram. Use variables.

proofs.title: Coordinate proof: the midsegment is parallel to the third side and half as long
proofs.given: △ABC with A(0, 0), B(2a, 0), C(2b, 2c). M is the midpoint of AC and N is the midpoint of BC.
steps: M = (b, c) and N = (a + b, c)
Slope of MN = (c − c)/((a + b) − b) = 0
Lines with equal slopes are parallel
proofs.idea: Doubling the coordinates (2a, 2b, 2c) removes fractions from the midpoints.
proofs.deep: Compare with the synthetic proof via similar triangles. Coordinates trade clever drawing for mechanical computation, which is often easier on a test.
proofs.trap: If you pick B = (a, 0) you get fractions everywhere. Choose coordinates so midpoints come out clean.

proofs.title: Two distinct lines intersect in at most one point (indirect proof)
proofs.given: ℓ and m are distinct lines.
proofs.prove: ℓ and m intersect in at most one point
steps: Assume ℓ and m intersect in two different points P and Q
P and Q are on both lines
Exactly one line passes through P and Q
ℓ and m are the same line
Both pass through P and Q
This contradicts the given fact that ℓ and m are distinct
ℓ and m intersect in at most one point
proofs.idea: In an indirect proof, assume the opposite and chase it until it contradicts something you know.
proofs.deep: The three parts of any indirect proof: assume the negation, derive a contradiction with a given or a known fact, conclude the original statement.
proofs.trap: The negation of “at most one” is “at least two”, not “exactly two”. Here “two points” is enough to find the contradiction.

proofs.title: There are infinitely many primes (Euclid, Honors)
proofs.given: A prime is a whole number greater than 1 whose only positive divisors are 1 and itself.
proofs.prove: The list of primes never ends
steps: Assume there are only finitely many primes p₁, p₂, …, pₙ
N has a prime factor q
Every whole number greater than 1 has a prime factor
q is one of p₁, …, pₙ
q divides p₁·p₂·…·pₙ and q divides N, so q divides 1
If q divides two numbers it divides their difference
proofs.idea: Multiply all the primes together and add 1. The new number cannot be divisible by any prime on the list.
proofs.deep: This is one of the oldest indirect proofs (about 300 BCE). It does not claim N is prime; it only shows N has a prime factor outside the list.
proofs.trap: N = (product) + 1 is not always prime. For example 2·3·5·7·11·13 + 1 = 30031 = 59·509.

proofs.title: The interior angles of an n-gon add to (n − 2)·180° (Honors)
proofs.given: A convex polygon with n sides.
steps: Pick one vertex and draw all diagonals from it
The polygon is divided into n − 2 triangles
Counting: the two sides touching the vertex are not used
The angles of each triangle add to 180°
The triangles’ angles together make up the polygon’s interior angles
proofs.idea: Cut the polygon into triangles from one vertex and count them.
proofs.deep: Check small cases: a quadrilateral (n = 4) gives 360°, a pentagon 540°. For a regular n-gon each angle is (n − 2)·180°/n. The exterior angles always add to 360°.
proofs.trap: Draw diagonals from ONE vertex only. Drawing from several vertices makes triangles that overlap.

proofs.title: The median to the base of an isosceles triangle is also an altitude
proofs.given: △ABC with AB = AC. D is the midpoint of BC.
steps: Congruent angles that form a linear pair are right angles
proofs.idea: SSS gives congruent triangles; CPCTC gives equal angles at D; a linear pair of equal angles is two right angles.
proofs.deep: The same figure shows AD also bisects ∠A. In an isosceles triangle the median, altitude, angle bisector and perpendicular bisector from the apex all coincide.
proofs.trap: In an equilateral triangle this happens from all three vertices. In a scalene triangle none of these lines coincide.

lessons.title: Undo, in reverse · Variables on both sides

cards.t: To solve an equation, undo what was done to x, in reverse order. Whatever you do to one side, do to the other.

lab.hook: Solve 2x + 3 = 11 by doing the same thing to both sides.
lab.take: Whatever you do to one side, do to the other.

cards.t: Move the x terms to one side and the numbers to the other. Then divide by the coefficient.

lab.hook: Where do the two lines meet? That x solves the equation.

cards.t: Multiply the number outside the parentheses by EVERY term inside. Then solve like normal.

lessons.title: Fractions in equations · Flip the sign

cards.t: Multiply every term by the denominator to clear the fraction. That keeps the equation balanced.
In an inequality, multiplying or dividing by a NEGATIVE flips the sign. Adding and subtracting never flips it.
Treat the other letters like numbers and undo operations in reverse. Formulas work the same way.
Slope tells how steep a line is: rise over run. Up-right is positive; down-right is negative.

lab.hook: Slope is rise over run. Change it and watch the steepness.
lab.out: Rise {m} for every 1 across. Positive goes up, negative goes down.

pre.q: Which line is steeper: slope 3 or slope 1?
pre.why: A bigger slope rises more for each step across.

cards.t: In y = mx + b, m is the slope and b is where the line crosses the y-axis.

lab.hook: y = mx + b: m tilts the line, b lifts it.
lab.out: y = {m}x + {b}. It crosses the y-axis at {b}.

cards.h: Make a line from a point
cards.t: Use the slope and a point to find b: plug x and y into y = mx + b, then solve for b.
Parallel lines have the same slope. Perpendicular slopes multiply to −1 (negative reciprocals).
Ax + By = C. To graph it, find the x- and y-intercepts by setting the other variable to 0.
In a word problem, slope is the rate (per hour, per item) and b is the starting amount.
A solution of a system is the point that makes BOTH equations true. On a graph it is where the lines cross.

lab.hook: A solution to a system is where the lines cross.
lab.out: The solution is the crossing point.

cards.t: Solve one equation for a letter, then plug that into the other equation. Best when a letter is already alone.
Add or subtract the equations so a letter cancels. Multiply an equation first if needed.

lessons.title: No or infinite solutions · Check your answer

cards.t: Parallel lines (same slope, different b) give NO solution. Same line gives infinitely many.
Plug your (x, y) into BOTH original equations. If both work, you are done.

lessons.title: Multiply, same base · Power of a power

cards.t: When multiplying powers with the same base, ADD the exponents.

lab.hook: Same base: add the exponents.

cards.t: For (xᵃ)ᵇ, MULTIPLY the exponents. Also raise every factor inside the parentheses.
When dividing, SUBTRACT the exponents (top minus bottom).
Anything (not 0) to the 0 is 1. A negative exponent means flip to the other side of the fraction.
Write a number as a × 10ⁿ with 1 ≤ a < 10. Moving the decimal left makes n bigger.

lessons.title: Factor out the GCF · Trinomials x² + bx + c

cards.t: Find the biggest number and letters shared by every term and pull them out. Always do this first.
Find two numbers that multiply to c and add to b. They go in the two parentheses.

lab.hook: Factors show where the parabola crosses the x-axis.

cards.t: a² − b² always factors into (a − b)(a + b). There must be a minus sign between two squares.
For ax² + bx + c, try the product a·c and split the middle term, then group.
If a product equals 0, one factor must be 0. Set each factor equal to 0 and solve.
√a asks: what number times itself gives a? Perfect squares: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81, 100.

lab.hook: A square root finds the side of a square from its area.

cards.t: Pull out the biggest perfect square factor. √72 = √36 · √2 = 6√2.
√a · √b = √(ab). You can also split a root of a fraction into top and bottom.
Only LIKE radicals combine, just like like terms. Simplify first.
If a root is left in the denominator, multiply top and bottom by that root.
f(x) is the output for input x. To find f(3), replace every x with 3 and calculate.
The graph of y = ax² + bx + c is a parabola. If a > 0 it opens up; if a < 0, down.

lab.hook: Every parabola has the same shape; a squeezes it or flips it.
lab.out: a = {a}. Positive opens up, negative opens down.

cards.t: The vertex is the turning point. Its x-coordinate is −b/(2a). Plug in to get y.

lab.hook: The vertex is the turning point.

cards.t: Move everything to one side, factor, set each factor to 0.
When factoring fails, use the formula. The discriminant b² − 4ac tells how many real solutions.
Repeated percent change uses A = P(1 + r)ⁿ. Decay uses (1 − r).
Arithmetic adds the same number each time; geometric multiplies by the same number.
|x| is the distance from 0. |x − 3| = 5 means x is 5 away from 3, so two answers.

lessons.title: Point, line, plane · Segment and ray

cards.t: A point is a location. A line goes on forever in two directions. A plane is a flat surface that goes on forever.
A segment has two endpoints. A ray has one endpoint and goes on forever. Name a ray with its endpoint first.
An angle has a vertex and two sides. Acute < 90°, right = 90°, obtuse between 90° and 180°, straight = 180°.
Complementary add to 90°. Supplementary add to 180°. A linear pair is two adjacent angles that make a straight line.

lab.hook: Angles that sit on a straight line add to 180°.

cards.t: When two lines cross, the angles directly across from each other are equal.
A midpoint splits a segment into two equal parts. A bisector splits a segment or angle in half.
Reflexive: a = a. Symmetric: if a = b then b = a. Transitive: if a = b and b = c then a = c. Substitution lets you swap equals.
'If p, then q.' p is the hypothesis and q is the conclusion. A statement is true only if it can never fail.
Converse: swap p and q. Inverse: negate both. Contrapositive: swap AND negate. Only the contrapositive always matches the original.
One example that makes the hypothesis true and the conclusion false proves a statement false.
Inductive finds a pattern from examples and may be wrong. Deductive uses facts to reach a sure conclusion, like in a proof.
Each statement needs a reason: given, definition, postulate or theorem. Start with the givens; finish with what you prove.
Assume the opposite of what you want. Show it leads to a contradiction. Then the original must be true.

lessons.title: Parallel lines and a transversal · Same-side interior

cards.t: A transversal crosses two lines and makes 8 angles. With parallel lines, corresponding, alternate interior and alternate exterior angles are EQUAL.
Same-side interior angles between parallel lines add to 180°. Z shape means equal, C shape means supplementary.
The converses work: if corresponding or alternate interior angles are equal, the lines are parallel.

lessons.title: Angle sum in a triangle · Polygon angles

cards.t: The three angles of a triangle always add to 180°. An exterior angle equals the sum of the two remote interior angles.

lab.hook: Angles in any triangle always add to 180°.

pre.q: A triangle has angles 60° and 50°. The third angle is…

cards.t: Interior angle sum = (n − 2) × 180°. Exterior angles of any convex polygon add to 360°.

lab.hook: More sides, more angle total.
lab.note: A {n}-sided shape has angles totalling {=(n-2)*180|0}°. Each regular angle: {=(n-2)*180/n|1}°.

cards.t: A regular polygon has equal sides and equal angles. Each exterior angle = 360° ÷ n.

lessons.title: Congruent triangles · Four ways to prove it

cards.t: Congruent triangles are the same shape AND size. Matching parts are called corresponding parts.
SSS, SAS, ASA and AAS prove congruence. For right triangles, HL works. AAA and SSA do NOT.
After you prove triangles congruent, ALL their matching parts are congruent. This is how you prove segments or angles equal.
Equal sides have equal angles opposite them, and the other way around. The bisector of the vertex angle is also a median and an altitude.
A median goes to a midpoint, an altitude is perpendicular, an angle bisector splits an angle. The medians meet at the centroid.
Any two sides add to MORE than the third. The longest side is opposite the largest angle.
Perpendicular bisectors meet at the circumcenter; angle bisectors at the incenter; altitudes at the orthocenter.
Opposite sides are parallel and equal, opposite angles are equal, consecutive angles add to 180°, diagonals bisect each other.
Show ONE of: both pairs of opposite sides equal, one pair both parallel and equal, or diagonals bisect each other.
A parallelogram with four right angles. Its diagonals are equal.
A parallelogram with four equal sides. Its diagonals are perpendicular and bisect the angles.
A square is both a rectangle and a rhombus, so it has every one of those properties.
One pair of parallel sides (bases). The midsegment is parallel to the bases and equals their average.
Two pairs of equal adjacent sides. One diagonal is the perpendicular bisector of the other.
A ratio compares two numbers. A proportion says two ratios are equal. Cross-multiply to solve.
Same shape, different size. Corresponding angles are equal and corresponding sides are in the same ratio (the scale factor).
AA is enough. Also SAS∼ (two sides in proportion, included angle equal) and SSS∼ (all three sides in proportion).
A line parallel to one side of a triangle cuts the other two sides in proportion.
An angle bisector in a triangle divides the opposite side in the same ratio as the two sides next to it.
If the scale factor is k, perimeters scale by k and areas scale by k². Volumes scale by k³.

lab.hook: Scale a shape by k. Perimeter scales by k, area by k².

cards.t: In a right triangle, the legs squared add to the hypotenuse squared. The hypotenuse is opposite the right angle.

lab.hook: Legs a and b make a right triangle. Find the long side.

pre.q: Legs 3 and 4. The long side is…

cards.t: Whole-number triples show up often: 3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17, 7-24-25. Multiples work too.
The legs are equal and the hypotenuse is leg × √2.
Short leg x, long leg x√3, hypotenuse 2x.
In a right triangle, the altitude to the hypotenuse is the geometric mean of the two pieces. Each leg is the geometric mean of the hypotenuse and its adjacent piece.
SOH-CAH-TOA: sin = opp/hyp, cos = adj/hyp, tan = opp/adj. Label sides from the angle you are using.

lab.hook: Resize the triangle, change the angle, watch the ratios.

cards.t: Both angles are measured from the horizontal. They make alternate interior angles, so they are equal.

lessons.title: Circle vocabulary · Central angles and arcs

cards.t: Radius: center to the circle. Chord: two points on the circle. Diameter: chord through the center. Tangent: touches once. Secant: cuts twice.
A central angle has the same measure as its arc. A full circle is 360°.
An inscribed angle is HALF its intercepted arc. An angle in a semicircle is 90°.

lab.hook: The center angle is twice the angle on the edge.

lessons.title: Tangents · Angles with chords and secants

cards.t: A tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of touching. Two tangents from one outside point are equal.
Inside the circle: half the SUM of the arcs. Outside: half the DIFFERENCE of the arcs.
Two chords: part × part = part × part. Tangent: (tangent)² = whole secant × outside part.

lessons.title: The tools · Copy a segment or angle

cards.t: Classic constructions use only a compass and straightedge. The compass copies equal lengths.
Set the compass to the length and mark it off. For an angle, copy the arc and the chord that cuts it.
Arcs from both ends with equal radii cross at two points. The line through them is the perpendicular bisector.

lessons.title: Perpendicular and parallel · What is a locus?

cards.t: Use equal arcs to make a perpendicular from a point. Copying a corresponding angle makes a parallel line.
A locus is ALL points that satisfy a rule. Equidistant from two points: a perpendicular bisector. At distance r from a point: a circle.
To satisfy two rules, draw each locus and mark where they cross. Count the intersections.
Rectangle: length × width. Parallelogram: base × height, where height is perpendicular to the base.
A triangle is half of a parallelogram. Use any side as the base with its matching height.

lab.hook: A triangle is half of a rectangle.

cards.t: Average the two bases and multiply by the height.
Area = ½ × apothem × perimeter. The apothem goes from the center to the middle of a side.
Circumference = 2πr. Area = πr². Keep π in your answer for an exact value.

lab.hook: Circle area grows with radius squared.

cards.t: A sector is a fraction of the circle: angle/360. Multiply that fraction by the area or circumference.
If lengths scale by k, area scales by k².

lessons.title: Prisms and cylinders · Pyramids and cones

cards.t: Volume = base area × height. Lateral area is the sides only; total surface area adds the bases.
Volume is one third of a prism or cylinder with the same base and height.
Surface area 4πr². Volume (4/3)πr³.

lessons.title: Lateral and total area · Similar solids

cards.t: Cylinder lateral area = 2πrh. Total area adds two circles: 2πr² + 2πrh.
With scale factor k, surface areas scale by k² and volumes by k³.
Pyramids and cones use the slant height for lateral area. Find it with the Pythagorean theorem.
The distance between two points comes from the Pythagorean theorem.

lab.hook: Distance is the Pythagorean theorem on the grid.

cards.t: Average the x's and average the y's.
Rise over run. Parallel lines have equal slopes. Perpendicular lines have slopes that multiply to −1.
Center (h, k), radius r. Note the signs: the center's coordinates are subtracted.
Place a figure on axes with smart coordinates (a vertex at the origin). Use distance, slope or midpoint to prove properties.
Check side lengths and slopes. Equal and parallel opposite sides → parallelogram. Add right angles → rectangle.
Translations, reflections and rotations keep size and shape. A dilation keeps shape but changes size.
Slide every point the same way. Add the shift to each coordinate.
Flip over a line. Over the x-axis: (x, −y). Over the y-axis: (−x, y). Over y = x: (y, x).
Turn about a point. About the origin: 90° → (−y, x), 180° → (−x, −y), 270° → (y, −x).
A figure has line symmetry if a flip maps it onto itself. It has rotational symmetry if a turn less than 360° maps it onto itself.
A dilation multiplies coordinates by the scale factor k. Doing transformations one after another is a composition.

lab.hook: A dilation scales every length by the same factor.
